title: NRT vs TypeScript strictNullChecks (compile-time only)
hook: Both C# NRT and TypeScript strictNullChecks are compile-time stories. The CLR still has null references. V8 still has null and undefined. A green build is not a proof that Redis returned a session.

sections.heading: What is the same
sections.prose: Enable the mode, annotate types, let flow analysis warn. string in a nullable-aware C# project is “should not be null,” like string under strictNullChecks. string? is “might be null,” like string | null. Optional chaining and nullish coalescing exist in both. The non-null assertion ! exists in both and is equally dishonest if you did not prove the value. JSON.parse in TS and System.Text.Json in C# both produce values the type checker believes if you asserted a type — neither inspects the wire. That is why an auth JWT deserializer is a runtime concern in both languages.

snippets.label: Same lie, two compilers
snippets.explanation: The bang and the TS assertion both shut the checker up. Redis or SQS still can hand you {}. Validate at the boundary.

sections.heading: What is different
sections.prose: C# value types cannot be null unless you wrap them in Nullable<T>. TypeScript number is already nullable in the JS sense only after you union it; at run time it is a IEEE-754 value or undefined. C# has no undefined. C# NRT does not erase to a different runtime, but the CLR still enforces that you cannot store a string in an int field — types survive in metadata. TypeScript erases completely. C# generic nullability needs MaybeNull; TypeScript uses T | undefined more freely because there is no Nullable<T> struct. Variance of nullability in generics is a C# warning minefield (notnull constraint in module 09) that TS solves with union distribution.

sections.heading: What you say in a mixed-stack interview
sections.prose: A one-liner: strictNullChecks and NRT are cousins — both compile-time, both optional historically, both on by default in new templates/tsconfig strict. Then add the C# exclusive: Nullable<T> is a CLR type, and NullReferenceException is a real runtime exception you still design for at SQS, CSV, Redis, and JWT edges. Do not claim C# is ‘null-safe’ the way a language with no null references is. Do not claim TypeScript is safer because it has undefined; that is two failure modes, not a type system win.

interviewTakeaways: NRT and strictNullChecks: compiler warnings, no runtime rewrite of reference types.
C# still has Nullable<T> and NRE; TS still has null, undefined, and TypeError.
Wire formats (JSON, Redis strings, SQS bodies) are untyped until you validate.
commonPitfalls: Saying ‘C# 8 made null impossible.’ It made warnings possible.
Equating undefined with int? — different machines.
Trusting Deserialize<T>() or as T because the DTO properties are non-nullable in source.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Closest analogue to <Nullable>enable</Nullable>. Both vanish at emit; both use ! as an escape hatch.
obj.foo when obj is null is TypeError in JS and NullReferenceException in C#. Optional chaining is the shared mitigation.
